chapter.title: What it owns: assets, fast and slow

cards.body: Which would you rather own on a bad morning: a $300,000 house or $300,000 in the bank? Same number, very different mornings. The cash pays the plumber at 9am; the house takes months to sell. A balance sheet lists what a company owns in exactly that order, **fastest to turn into cash at the top, slowest at the bottom**, and the line between them is 12 months.
cards.simpler: Imagine you own a house worth $300,000. Now imagine you have $300,000 sitting in the bank instead. The number is the same, but the money is not. Cash can pay a plumber this morning. A house takes months to sell. A company's list of what it owns works the same way. It runs **fastest to turn into cash at the top, slowest at the bottom**. The dividing line is 12 months.

cards.prompt: Dev runs a bakery. She owns three things: $4,000 in the till, 200 bags of flour, and one big oven. Which is the slowest to turn into cash?

whyNot.a: That's already cash, not something that needs turning into cash: nothing on the sheet is faster than money in the till.
whyNot.b: That's stock, not a slow asset: flour becomes bread, and bread becomes cash, within weeks.

cards.reteach: Ask: if Dev needed money by next month, what could she sell without breaking the business? The till money is instant. The flour sells as bread. The oven would take months to sell and leave her with nothing to bake in. Fast sits at the top of the list, slow at the bottom.

cards.title: Fast: the top half
cards.body:
The top half of the asset list is called *current assets*: things that are cash now or should become cash within 12 months. Three lines do most of the work. *Cash* is the money in the bank. *Inventory* is stock waiting to be sold: flour in the bakery, phones in a warehouse. *Receivables* are bills the company has sent to customers that are not yet paid.

In the house picture, this is the drawer of notes, the food in the fridge, and the $50 your neighbour still owes you for the fence. **All three should be money within a year.** Receivables are the one to watch. A bill sent is not a bill paid.
cards.simpler: The top half of the list is called current assets. These are things that are cash now or should turn into cash within 12 months. Cash is money in the bank. Inventory is stock waiting to be sold, like flour in a bakery. Receivables are bills the company has sent to customers who have not paid yet. **All three should be money within a year.** Watch the receivables. A bill sent is not a bill paid.

cards.title: Marta's bike shop, 31 December
cards.body: Cash in the bank: $12,000. Bikes on the shop floor, at what she paid for them: $48,000. Invoices sent to the city council for 30 delivery bikes, still unpaid: $22,000. Her current assets total $82,000, but **only $12,000 of it could pay a bill tomorrow**. The council pays in 90 days, if it pays on time, and the bikes only become money when someone walks in and wants one. Marta looks rich on paper and checks her bank app twice a day.
cards.simpler: Marta has $12,000 in the bank. Her bikes, at what she paid, come to $48,000. Unpaid bills sent to the city council for 30 delivery bikes come to $22,000. Her current assets total $82,000. But **only $12,000 of it could pay a bill tomorrow**. The council pays in 90 days, if it pays on time. The bikes only become money when a customer buys one. Marta looks rich on paper and checks her bank app twice a day.

cards.prompt: A software company's balance sheet shows four assets: an office building ($5m), unpaid customer invoices ($2m), cash ($1m), and a brand it bought from a rival ($3m). Which two lines are current, meaning fast, assets?

options.text: The unpaid invoices and the bought brand

whyNot.b: That's mixing a fast asset with a slow one: the building would take months to sell, and the company needs it to work in.
whyNot.c: That's mixing a fast asset with a slow one: a bought brand never turns into cash by itself, so it sits at the bottom.

cards.reteach: Current means cash within 12 months. Cash already is cash. Invoices should be paid in weeks. A building and a bought brand are kept for years: useful, but not money any time soon, so they go in the slow half.

cards.title: Slow: the bottom half
cards.body:
Below the line sit *non-current assets*, the slow ones: things the company plans to keep and use for years. *Property, plant and equipment* is the stuff you could kick: buildings, machines, delivery vans. Then come *intangibles*, things you cannot touch: software, patents, and a brand or customer list bought from another company, which often shows up as *goodwill*.

You'd think the solid half is the safer half. In one way it's the opposite: **the number next to a slow asset is a cost, not a price**. The van is listed at what was paid, minus wear. Goodwill is listed at what a buyer once hoped it was worth. Neither tells you what someone would pay tonight.
cards.simpler: Below the line sit non-current assets, the slow ones the company keeps for years. Property, plant and equipment means buildings, machines, vans. Intangibles are things you cannot touch: software, patents, and a bought brand, often listed as goodwill. **The number next to a slow asset is a cost, not a price.** The van is listed at what was paid, minus wear. Goodwill is what a buyer once hoped it was worth. Neither says what someone would pay tonight.

cards.body: Tomasz reads a retailer's balance sheet, sees $900m of total assets, and relaxes. He never looked down the list: $600m of it is goodwill from buying a rival chain, and cash is $15m. The way to spot this is to **cover the total and read the top three lines by size**. If the biggest thing the company owns is something it cannot touch or sell, it owns less than the total suggests.
cards.simpler: Tomasz reads a retailer's balance sheet. He sees $900m of total assets and relaxes. He never reads down the list. $600m of that total is goodwill from buying a rival chain. Cash is only $15m. The way to catch this is to **cover the total and read the top three lines by size**. If the biggest thing a company owns is something it cannot touch or sell, it owns less than the total suggests.

cards.prompt: On a balance sheet, the asset lines run from top to bottom in order of what?

options.text: How fast each one turns into cash

whyNot.a: That's how you'd rank them for size, not how the sheet orders them: a tiny cash line still sits above a huge building.
whyNot.c: That's purchase history, not the sheet's rule: a van bought yesterday still sits below invoices sent last year.

cards.reteach: Picture the house. Cash in the drawer first, food in the fridge next, money the neighbour owes you after that. Then the car, then the house itself. The sheet orders assets by how soon they become money, and draws its line at 12 months.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
A company's assets are listed **fastest to slowest**: cash, stock and unpaid customer bills at the top should be money within 12 months, while buildings, machines and bought brands at the bottom are kept for years. The top half pays this year's bills; the bottom half's numbers are old costs, not today's prices.

Tomorrow: a company can owe billions and be perfectly healthy. The trick is when.
cards.simpler: A company lists what it owns **fastest to slowest**. At the top sit cash, stock, and unpaid customer bills. These should be money within 12 months. At the bottom sit buildings, machines, and brands bought from other companies. These are kept for years. The top half pays this year's bills. The bottom half's numbers are old costs, not today's prices. Tomorrow: a company can owe billions and still be perfectly healthy. The trick is when.

cards.body: Search online for any company's annual report, find the page titled balance sheet, and read the asset lines top to bottom. Write down the **three biggest** and mark each one F for fast or S for slow.
cards.simpler: Search online for any company's annual report. Find the page called balance sheet. Read the asset lines from top to bottom. Write down the **three biggest** by size. Next to each one, write F if it is fast, meaning it should become cash within a year, or S if it is slow, meaning the company keeps it for years.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now sort every asset line into fast or slow and name the two or three biggest things a company owns.
